en: Preface to the Suspended Mirror of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra *Śūraṃgama* is the general name for the Great Samādhi. However, those in the world who receive this sūtra harbor two kinds of uncertainty regarding its lack of fixity.
The first concerns the uncertainty of the transmission of the sūtra. At the beginning of the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Prajñāmitra...
Concealing it, he privately brought the Sanskrit manuscript to Guangzhou, where he translated it and bestowed it upon the State Councilor Fang Rong.

At that time, his own country censured him for violating regulations; he fled while carrying the manuscript. Rong also submitted a memorial regarding it, but it was not implemented. Externally, there was no evidence of the Sanskrit original;
internally, it was missing from the catalogues. Thus, doubts already could not be dispelled. Furthermore, Zhisheng stated that the śramaṇa Huaidi encountered [the text].
A Brahman monk translated it together [with others] at Guangzhou in ten fascicles; when compared with the version by Daorong, there was not the slightest difference.

Could it be that Daodi was receiving the oral transmission alongside Daorong? Such lack of detail in Zhi Sheng’s record makes it difficult to transmit as authoritative. Furthermore, when we examine the historical record:
Faxian recited it during the Jin dynasty, Fachong upheld it during the Liang dynasty, and Zhiyi could not find it during the Sui dynasty.
Yet Daorong and others first received it from the Tang dynasty;

whether from that source or this, whether hidden or manifest, the uncertainty regarding the transmission of this scripture gives rise to the first doubt among later generations. Second is the uncertainty of its classification:

while the designations of the five periods and four teachings encompass all scriptures such that each is invariably categorized according to them, this particular scripture is the most difficult to classify.

Master Huan judged it to belong within the *Prajñāpāramitā*; Master Xuan judged it to belong within the *Vaipulya*. Masters Zhi and Yuan and others judged it to fall between the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Now, one who has not ended their life prematurely yet has not attained the *dharmakāya* does not possess the *prajñā*.

To have shattered the "external naturalism" on Mount Laṅkā is not the domain of the *vaipulya*. As for King Bimbisāra and his son, they were born before the year they were to receive their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
It is neither the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* nor the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

It is not gradual, not sudden, not esoteric, not indeterminate, and not categorized as *zàng*, *tōng*, *bié*, or *yuán*, as listed in the *Zhēnjué bǎiwèn* (One Hundred Questions on True Awakening). From beginning to end, its sequence is hazy and difficult to rely upon;
thus, its scriptural classification is unsettled, giving rise to doubts among later generations—this is the second point. Xuānsǎ often cited what Master Xiù experienced within the inner dharma-hall.
I have recorded the sincere words of Master Miao (Mingxiao), who used the character of the former Chancellor’s family to explain the doubts regarding the transmission of the sutra.
I privately believe that if the world trusts these two masters, it will likewise trust this sutra without confusion.

Now, if the fourfold assembly trusts Master Han as they did those two masters, would it not be insufficient to judge [this teaching] as not being the sudden revelation of a single moment? It is surely worthy of trust.
The discourse at Śrāvastī was given at one time; the discourse at Kapilavastu was likewise at another time.

The compilers of the canon intended merely to manifest the meaning of the single mind and its threefold contemplation—how the ten periods of past and present do not depart from the present moment—and how could such examples be used to restrict this?
Nevertheless, the Master has already revealed the true mind and clarified the great samādhi almost exhaustively.
It is indeed so. Furthermore, must it not have a specific significance that this is necessarily named the "Hanging Mirror"?
The mirror suspended in space and illuminating the altar is, in fact, the ritual protocol for upholding the *citta-mantra* (mind-mantra).

In the past, Ānanda and the Mātanga woman, by means of this mind-mantra, cultivated through a single thought-moment and transcended the outflows to realize the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The World-Honored One was about to...
Desiring to expound the Great Dharani, he first followed his habit of extensive learning by providing various explanations.
He then excised the manifold teachings he had heard regarding the Buddha’s words as they were spoken to the fourfold assembly, including those concerning Mañjuśrī and the bhikṣu Mahāmati.
This caused him to become composed, expansive, clear, and lucid, until finally he attained a state of joyful liberation within this Vajra.
The secret of the Samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation can only be explained through divine mantras. Thus, Avalokiteśvara is the one who is truly suited to this practice;

therefore, having examined all modes of penetration, he selected the sound of his Brahma-voice and the sound of the tide—whereby one form and one mantra may be used for cultivation and realization—as the Dharma.
Cultivating in this way and realizing in this way, one attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Vajra-mind.
Each stage and every stage is observed with the diamond-like mind; this diamond-like mind and diamond-like observation is the diamond samādhi.

From dawn until dusk, sounds are linked together as they enter through the faculty of hearing. Entering by way of these gates, one attains dhāraṇī and gains entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Were it otherwise—if the mind had not yet attained penetration—it would mean that the Buddha speaks falsely.
If Māra has not yet been subdued, then the recitation of mantras would be in vain. Do you not observe the five names established by the World-Honored One himself?
They are: Ratnamudrā (Precious Seal), Paritrāṇa (Protection), Guhyahetu (Secret Cause), and finally, Dhāraṇī-mantra-abhiṣeka-pada (Dhāra� Master’s Mantra for Consecration).
This term "abhiṣeka" (consecration) appears three or four times throughout the sutra. Master Yue judged this to be the Indian consecration.
At the very top [of the text], it is clearly evident from what is transmitted in the Tripiṭaka that this must be the Secret Mantra (Vajrayāna).

How could this perfectly round ocean of fruition have temporal limits such that it could be contained within a single period or a single teaching? Some may claim that there is no such explicit exposition among the five families of Secret Mantra;
yet they fail to realize that what is referred to as "Naya" (or *nyan thos*) is precisely "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). It is I who have heard it from the Buddha...
The sincere words from the Golden Mouth are indeed the *Abhiṣeka-mantra* (灌頂章句). Yet, how could it not be an error if one finds it difficult to believe, accept, and practice?
For this reason, Master Han accepted it and suspended it like a mirror.

Having obtained this *dhāraṇī-heart*, regardless of whether one ascends a blade or enters fire—even if Master An read the sutras with broken phrases or Master Gui slandered the Buddha with false claims—there is nothing that cannot be done; one must simply set aside [other practices] for the sake of the *dhāraṇī*.
To discuss the "true mind" while harboring a deluded mind is merely to increase one's erudition; it is not the intention of the World-Honored One, nor is it the intention of Master Han.
Written on the first day of the New Year in the Xinmao year of the Wanli era by the layman Yu Chunxi of Shizi Lin.
Preface to the Suspended Mirror of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
As for the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, it is the secret treasury of all Buddhas, the wondrous gateway to practice, the root-source of delusion and awakening, and the fundamental basis of the true and the false.
That which it expounds points directly to the single flavor of the pure Tathāgata.
The true mind is taken as the essence. This essence of the mind is fundamentally numinous, luminous, vast, profound, empty, tranquil, equal, and such-like;
it is free from all names and characteristics, where the holy and the ordinary are one boundary, and birth and Buddhahood are identical.
Yet, through delusion, birth and death become endless; through awakening, saṃsāra is suddenly stilled. Therefore, our Buddha realized this and took pity on those beings who are deluded.
Therefore, by assuming great authority, he initiated this teaching. He opened wide the gate of cultivation and realization, and skillfully showed the path home.
Thus, all that is expounded in this entire work—from beginning to end—does not transcend the two dharmas of delusion and enlightenment, or truth and falsehood.

Yet, while the paths of delusion are myriad in form and the gates of enlightenment are many, if one seeks to grasp the essence and exhaust the source, there is no lack of a vital point. As for following from delusion...

The method for ultimate awakening and the pointer toward returning the delusory to the true lies precisely in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* and the wondrous gate of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
If one wishes to penetrate and observe the Dharma-realm, thoroughly perceive one’s own mind, and directly return to the source by beholding its very essence, nothing is more essential than this.

Alas, the phrasing is concise and profound, and the principles are subtle and deep; although the commentaries and sub-commentaries of various masters have elucidated them with precision and clarity, students—

Greedy for progress, I was unaware of the shortcut; consequently, my contemplation of principle became obscured by stale clichés, and my cultivation failed to attain right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

Though pure, I did not measure my own rusticity, yet I have long devoted myself to this literature. Having cut off all external perceptions and endured the hardships of frost and snow, I consider my own intellect and knowledge to be dark and dim;
I do not dare to presume upon the Sage’s mind. Nevertheless, whenever there was a narrow path through which a thread of insight might pass, I have roughly set forth my humble views.

May those who cultivate in seclusion regard this as if looking into a mirror to observe their own forms; may they, by taking these matters as the occasion for settling the mind, suddenly realize the nature hidden within.
Written in the winter of the Bingxu year of the Wanli era by the dhūta Deqing of Mount Han, at the Nārāyaṇa Cave on the Eastern Sea.
The Hanging Mirror of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
Elucidating the Nārāyaṇa Cave of the Eastern Sea, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Deqing of Haiyin.

In order to facilitate a thorough understanding of its great meaning, this work is divided into two general chapters (the threefold great meaning is detailed separately in the General Discussion and is not listed here at length).
First, the great opening of the gateway for cultivation and realization (from the initial petition to the conclusion of the title);

second, the detailed exposition on the distinctions between delusion and awakening (from the thorough investigation of the seven realms of existence to the fifty layers of the demon of the aggregates).
Within the first [section], there are briefly four points of meaning.
First, it demonstrates the essence of the three contemplations; second, it demonstrates the characteristics of the three contemplations;
third, it demonstrates the function of the three contemplations; fourth, it concludes with the names of the three contemplations.
Regarding the four points within the initial opening of the gate of cultivation and realization: it is because the true source is profoundly still and quiescent, transcending birth and extinction.

The Dharma-realm is profound and mysterious, erasing the traces of sagehood and ordinariness. Fundamentally, there is neither cultivation nor realization; how could it belong to awakening or delusion?
Now, relying on delusion that is not delusive, we establish a cultivation that is without cultivation; thus there is a realization that is without realization.

For one who is deluded regarding the truth and pursues the false inevitably sinks into the current of birth and death. Now, wishing to turn back from the false and return to the true, one must establish practice based upon the truth.
This sutra takes the single-flavor, pure *dharmadhātu*, the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the true mind as its essence.
Based on this one mind, the three contemplations are established; by means of these three contemplations, one returns to realize the one mind. Therefore it is said:

"There is nothing that does not flow from this *dharmadhātu*, and there is nothing that does not return to this *dharmadhātu*. For this reason, Ānanda manifests as if he has not yet attained realization.

Having realized this mind, yet having not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) despite extensive learning, one is unable to suddenly uproot the source of birth and death, and consequently falls into the perilous trap of Māraṇḍa’s brothel.
For this reason, he earnestly requested the sublime gateway of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
Therefore, our World-Honored One first demonstrated that the single mind illuminates all phenomena, and at the outset declared: "All sentient beings..."
The continuity of death arises entirely from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity. Furthermore, it is said:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.
By examining these two statements, the purport of the entire scripture is clearly seen. Is this not intended to cause [the practitioner] first...
Having realized the one mind, one establishes the three contemplations based upon it; by practicing these three contemplations, one returns to realize the one mind.
As for my previous response, although I employed various methods of discernment and exhaustive investigation, everything was none other than a manifestation of the one mind.

It reveals the source of the Dharma and secretly sets forth the essence of the three contemplations (from the first fascicle to the middle of the fourth). Based upon this, one initiates practice and cultivation;
it introduces the methods for awakening and entry used by the twenty-five sages, and mandates that the faculty of hearing is precisely the primary expedient means.

(From the middle of the fourth fascicle to the beginning of the sixth fascicle) This causes the beginner who first sets their resolve to know that the observation of signs (*nimitta*) is distinct and clear.

Thereafter, by the natural functioning of the single mind (*ekacitta*), there spontaneously arise the various applications for severing delusions and realizing the Truth, according to their respective levels of depth.

(From the beginning of the seventh fascicle to the middle of the eighth fascicle) Because the cultivation and severance have reached their ultimate limit, he concludes by pointing to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*), ensuring that from beginning to end there is a single source that does not depart from the Great Samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*.
Therefore, I shall conclude by attaching [this commentary] to the title of the sutra; this is indeed the great purport of the general path.
First, the essence of the three contemplations is revealed, and this essence is what is called the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of intrinsic purity and luminosity.
This is precisely the one true *dharmadhātu*, the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
First, this essence is shown as the object of contemplation, for it is by relying upon this essence that the function of great wisdom is activated. Now, this *garbha*-mind possesses three aspects:
first, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*; second, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*; and third, the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Regarding the "single empty tathāgatagarbha": it means that the essence of this garbha is fundamentally empty, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended.

It is like a maṇi jewel whose substance is empty and pure, entirely devoid of color or form; yet although colors appear according to their surroundings, these colors do not exist apart from the jewel itself.

Because it is identical with the jewel, the true mind is fundamentally pure and completely transcends delusive conditions. Although there are delusions that follow along with conditions, these delusions do not depart from the truth;

because they are identical with the truth, it is called "True Emptiness" (zhēn kōng). Therefore, for the practitioner, the true mind is first revealed as the substance of contemplation. One who can contemplate this substance is said to practice the Contemplation of True Emptiness (zhēn kōng guān).

[The sutra names this *śamatha* and also the Cessation of the Substance-Truth (*tǐ zhēn zhǐ*)]. This begins from the beginning of the sutra... [A]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly at "阿" [A], which likely refers to the opening syllable of the title *Ārya-brahma-paripṛcchā-sūtra* or similar, though the specific context of the "beginning of the sutra" is not fully detailed in the fragment.)
It was difficult to request that the World-Honored One grant permission to speak, so he said:

"There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.

Following this, there are the seven investigations and eight arguments; beginning with the discernment of the real and the false, it first states that the false is not the real, thereby clarifying the body of the five aggregates.
The mind does not exist; the world is fundamentally empty. By shattering the dual attachments to self and dharmas, one reveals the true suchness of original enlightenment.
Through the three categories and seven groups of aggregates, one returns to the hidden nature. Only then do the real and the false harmoniously merge, revealing that the false is itself the real.
From the shallow to the profound, this first major section generally reveals the principle of the *śūnya-tathāgatagarbha* (from the beginning of the first fascicle to the end of the third).
Second, regarding the *aśūnya-tathāgatagarbha*: although the essence of this *garbha* is empty, it possesses merits numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges that accord with its nature;
it encompasses and integrates all things without omission, just as a *maṇi* jewel, though pure in its substance, possesses [all qualities].
The function of illumination is able to manifest all forms according to their respective directions; these forms are themselves the jewel.
Because they are manifested by the jewel, although the nature of the treasury is empty, it can manifest the appearances of the ten realms—the environment and its inhabitants—according to conditions.

These appearances are themselves the nature, for they arise from the nature. This is called "not being truly empty. Therefore, for the sake of the contemplator, this treasury-nature is shown as the essence of contemplation. It is able to...

Contemplating this essence is called the Contemplation of Non-Emptiness (the sutra title for this samādhi is also *Upāya-anuvartana-sthiti*). This section follows Pūrṇa’s challenge regarding the nature of phenomena based on their perceived characteristics.
It profoundly investigates the causes of the threefold continuity of existence and clearly elucidates the meaning of how things manifest according to karma.

It comprehensively reveals the essence of non-emptiness (beginning from the start of the fourth fascicle until the end of this fascicle; from "The wondrously enlightened luminous nature of True Suchness arises" onwards, there are half a fascicle of text, totaling approximately one thousand five hundred words).
The threefold emptiness and non-empty Tathāgatagarbha refers to this nature of the treasury, whose essence is pure and capable of responding and manifesting.

It is like a maṇi jewel, whose essence is pure and perfect. Because it is pure, it is not form; yet because it is the very jewel itself, it is not that it cannot respond as form, for it is identical with form.
It is neither form nor jewel. And so too is this nature of the treasury, its essence being pure and perfect. Because it is pure...
It is not non-characteristic because it is identical to nature; it is perfect because it can manifest as characteristics, yet it is not non-characteristic because it is identical to characteristics.

That which is neither characteristic nor nature is called "empty and non-empty": it is empty because it is not characteristics, and non-empty because it is not [merely] nature. Being neither identical to nor separate from [characteristics and nature], it is the equality of suchness; this is called the Middle Way.
Therefore, for the sake of the practitioner, this treasury-nature is revealed as the substance of contemplation, serving as the object of observation. It is that which is able to observe.

This essence is called the contemplation of the Middle Way (the sutra calls it *dhyāna*, also called the cessation that is free from the discrimination of the two extremes, and also called *samādhi*). This section, which begins with "The Tathāgatagarbha does not arise from mind, etc.

and concludes with "it is itself permanence, bliss, self, and purity," consists of two chapters and approximately three hundred words. It is excerpted from the fourth fascicle [of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*].

However, although the substance of the three aforementioned truths is non-dual, raising one necessarily implies the three; thus, they remain bound by names and concepts and still exist as distinct entities.
They have not yet reached the source of the single mind and are difficult to harmonize with the principle of perfect fusion.

Only if one transcends both "identity" and "non-identity"—neither identifying nor not identifying—then the wondrous nature of the storehouse-consciousness will exhaustively reach its source, severing all dualistic oppositions. This is because, when both are transcended...
Both are extinguished. When both are affirmed, both are preserved; when preserved, the three truths are luminously present; when extinguished, the one mind has no point of reliance.

Stillness and illumination are simultaneous; preservation and extinction are mutually unimpeded. This can only be realized through the spirit by those who have forgotten words, and penetrated through the mind by those who have severed all discursive thought.
It may be called a wondrous accord within the phenomenal world, where all is extinguished and made identical with the Dharma-realm. Perfectly interfused, perfectly interfused—contemplate this deeply.
Reflect deeply; it is vivid and unmistakable. Therefore, having completed his instruction, the Buddha addressed them collectively, saying:

"The principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature) explained above is thus profound and subtle. How can you, with your minds of discursive knowledge, fathom it, or through worldly language, enter into it?
Furthermore, this wondrous principle is inherently possessed by every person. Although it is originally present,"
It is fully present yet unmanifest. For example, although a lute or a zither possesses exquisite tones, they cannot be produced without skillful fingers;
likewise, although sentient beings possess an exquisite mind, it cannot be revealed without skillful contemplation.

Furthermore, as I now realize this true mind and abide in the Great Samādhi, illuminating the Dharma-realm with perfect clarity, every movement is the manifestation of its great function. You, however, are deluded.
Every movement, gesture, and action is merely the functioning of defiled labor (*saṃkleśa-karma*). Therefore, it is said: "When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal manifests its radiance;
when you briefly raise your mind, defiled labor arises first. This is for no other reason than that you are unwilling to seek diligently and are content with a mere trifle.
The practitioner then asked: "For what cause does delusion exist? [The Master replied: To reveal that delusion fundamentally has no cause, so as to bring about awakening.
The false does not depart from the true; it is like the head, which cannot be obtained from outside. Yet this natural, wondrous nature does not require cultivation to be perfected.

It is only by turning the light back for a single thought-moment that one awakens to the fact that the divine pearl is inherently present. Therefore, following the refutation of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), he earnestly exhorts practice and maintenance, saying:
"Though you may memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for a single day."

How can one deceive oneself by continuing to remain as a mere observer and listener without practicing? Therefore, upon hearing this teaching, Ānanda’s doubts were dispelled and his mind awakened to the true reality (*dharmatā*).

He subsequently requested entry into the "Flower House" (*puṣpavimāna*) to subdue his discursive attachments, hoping thereby to attain the *dhāraṇī* and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).
Viewed from this perspective, the general intent of the initial exposition of the *tathāgatagarbha* was surely to—

Does this mean that one first awakens to the One Mind and, based upon it, establishes the wondrous practice of the three contemplations, and only then, once practice is perfected and understanding is severed,
does one suddenly realize the One Mind?
This concludes the initial demonstration of the substance of the three contemplations, which belongs to the stage of the Path of Vision (darśana-mārga).
Second, regarding the demonstration of the characteristics of the three contemplations:
Because the previously revealed True Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata-garbha mind, possesses the meaning of vast wisdom and luminosity within its essential nature, it is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

Now, this wisdom, which is identical to that essence, shines back upon the tranquil, extinguished essence. When principle and wisdom are of one suchness, free from thought and free from marks, it is called "one mind."

The source is fundamentally without words or teachings. Now, by means of the gateway of true and false, arising and ceasing, we shall synthesize and grasp the path of returning to the true by reversing the false.
There are also three layers of skillful means established herein: because wisdom illuminates principle, it is simply termed "contemplation" (guan);
because it clarifies matters through the perspective of deluded appearances, it is called "contemplating appearances" (guanshang).
First, I shall briefly indicate the gates of contemplation:
first, the śamatha contemplation of emptiness; second, the samāpatti contemplation of non-emptiness;
and third, the dhyāna contemplation of the Middle Way.

First, regarding what is called "śamatha as the contemplation of emptiness": it means realizing that the one true dharma-realm, the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, is fundamentally without arising or ceasing and devoid of all characteristics.
It is because of a single moment of non-awakening that ignorance arises;
due to this ignorance, the three subtleties, the six coarsenesses, the four great elements, the six sense organs, and all manner of phenomena are produced. Yet, these phenomena are nothing but mind.
That which appears is fundamentally non-existent; it is merely the single mind.

The essence of the mind is perfectly luminous and free from all marks, just as colors within a jewel are originally non-existent because they are identical with emptiness. Therefore, it is said that "form is itself emptiness.

Because form is not [inherently] form, form does not differ from emptiness; thus it is called "true emptiness. One who practices this contemplation is said to practice the contemplation of true emptiness.
Regarding the second samāpatti, called the "Contemplation of Non-Emptiness": it means realizing that all phenomena—the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world—are but the one mind.
The essence of this mind is perfectly bright and pure by nature, pervading the entire dharma-realm, manifesting in accordance with conditions.

This means that all phenomena are, in their very essence, empty and illusory, lacking substantial reality. Just as colors within a gem appear clearly and distinctly, yet the entire gem is those very colors;
because it is identical to color, it is said that "emptiness is itself form. Because emptiness is not a [separate] emptiness, emptiness is not different from form;
therefore, it is called "non-empty. One who practices this contemplation is said to practice the contemplation of non-emptiness.
The third dhyāna is called "Middle Way Contemplation" (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*). This means that by relying on this quiescent single mind, one illuminates all phenomena (*dharma*).
All phenomena are inherently quiescent in their very essence. Because they are quiescent, they are "empty" (*śūnya*); because they are illuminated, they are "not empty.

Like a jewel and its color—neither the color nor the jewel is [separately] the jewel—it is called "empty and not empty. Being neither quiescent nor illuminating, it is suchness (*tathatā*) and equality, the single source of the one mind, profoundly still.
Yet it is immovable. It is neither "is" nor "is not," and it is both "is" and "is not. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases.

With mind following mind without interval, one flows spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). One who practices this contemplation is said to practice the contemplation of the Middle Way.
Next, in the section that correctly demonstrates the characteristics of contemplation, the main outline consists of four parts:
first, a general demonstration of the root of delusion and awakening; second, a correct demonstration of the characteristics of the threefold contemplation within the one mind;
third, a brief demonstration of the method for untying the knots; and fourth, an extensive demonstration of the initial expedient means.

First, the general indication of the root of delusion and awakening: Because Ānanda had previously heard the Buddha’s instruction, he had already realized that the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha—the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind—is perfect, pervasive, and fully present within himself, requiring no external seeking.

This was because he had hitherto merely engaged in the pursuit of external objects and failed to subdue his own mind; now, though he intends to contemplate and practice it, he does not know how to advance.
Regarding this method, there was the question of being invited into a magnificent mansion, hoping to find a direct and straightforward gate through which one might enter at once.
Because cultivation proceeds according to individual characteristics, this section is titled "The Characteristics of the Three Contemplations.

However, the World-Honored One taught no other method than first causing one to discern clearly between the true and the false, and thereafter providing appropriate treatment as the occasion demands. Thus, I wish to return [to that original intent].
The false returns to the true; the inception of this process does not go beyond the two definitive meanings.

This means that, fundamentally, one is deluded regarding this perfectly luminous, profound, and tranquil true mind, which then coalesces into the four great elements and falsely divides into the six sense organs. Through the conjunction of the organs and their objects, empty and false arising and ceasing occur.

It gives rise to the karmic functions and afflictions of the five turbidities, causing the wondrously perfect essence to become separated and obstructed—like various vessels placed within the great void.
The profoundly still and deep mind becomes turbid and loses its illumination, as if fine dust were cast into clear water.
Thus, that which was originally undivided becomes divided; that which was fundamentally unturbid becomes turbid. Now, wishing to [realize] this very arising and ceasing...
To realize the true and eternal, one must turn back from the illusory and restore the wondrous enlightenment.

First, one must take this mind of non-arising and non-perishing as the fundamental cause of cultivation to illuminate and shatter the source of arising and perishing. Next, one must examine the root from which [the faculties] were bound to determine which is the basis of affliction.

If one brings forth illumination upon the arising and ceasing of phenomena, then one immediately enters true permanence. If one knows the root of afflictions, they are resolved as easily as a blade slicing through meat.

Thus, the single mind that is capable of illuminating is such that every moment of mind is quiescent and extinguished; the myriad dharmas that are illuminated are such that every dharma is perfectly interfused and unobstructed.
Thus, one suddenly transcends the five turbidities and returns to the original unity. If one takes this as the causal mind, the fruit of realization can be perfected.
Now, although the single mind that is deluded is inherently perfect and all-pervasive, the manifest functions of the six faculties that cause delusion are not uniform.

Next, the distinctions between delusion and awakening are shown in detail.
The preceding exposition has thoroughly revealed the true source of the single mind; the subtle purport of the three contemplations is fully understood.

The states of delusion and awakening have been entirely set forth, and the conditions of ordinary beings and sages are exhausted. Nevertheless, delusion arises from a single thought, where emotional perceptions erupt in disorder, leading to the ascent and descent within the seven realms of existence.
Awakening rests upon the single mind, yet through the horizontal proliferation of false views, one encounters the demons of the five aggregates.
This is what is meant by "disturbance": the self-mind grasping at the self-mind, whereby that which is not illusory becomes illusory phenomena.

Therefore, our World-Honored One, moved by genuine compassion, felt such deep pain that he would have plucked out his gallbladder and carved out his heart. He meticulously investigated the causes of the seven destinies, distinguishing between internal and external states according to the variations in emotional thought;
he analyzed the demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) in detail, revealing how the depths of mind-contemplation differ based on deluded views. This is why it is so.
This is simply to urge us to contemplate the suffering of the hells and give rise to the bodhicitta; to know that there is nirvana and not to cling to the triple world.

Alas, O people!
